reason: 'Indistinctly delimited' means the boundaries are unclear. PATO inconspicuous (PATO_0000464) is about visibility, not about distinct edges. No existing class means 'without a clear boundary'.
A short-exserted part still sticks out, so exserted (PATO_0000623) is true. Only the degree is lost. A correct broader class is better than no annotation.

Glossaries define crinite either as having long weak hairs or as having tufts of long hairs. Bearded (FLOPO_0991118, a tuft or zone) fits only the second, and villous fits only the first. Hairy, the parent of both, is true under either reading.
'Bunch' is a noun (a bunch of fruit or flowers). It does not say that stems grow in a dense tuft from the base, which is what caespitose (FLOPO_0991007) means.
A scabrid-denticulate margin is rough because of its tiny teeth. Scabrous (FLOPO_0991058: rough from small stiff projections) is true of it. The teeth are lost, but the class is not wrong.

On a calyx reduced to a rim on top of the ovary, or on a disc, 'rimlike' describes a ring around the top: ring shaped (PATO_0002539, also called annular). On other parts it means a raised edge, which is not a ring.
Hummock grasses (e.g. Triodia) form mounds and are told apart from tussock grasses. Neither caespitose (FLOPO_0991007) nor mat-forming (FLOPO_0991010) fits, and no mound or cushion class exists.
'Tolerant to' (PATO_0000515) needs the thing tolerated. Without 'drought' the statement says nothing. It needs a pattern that records the stimulus, not a word rule.

Umbelliform (FLOPO_0991031) is defined for inflorescences, and cymes arranged in an umbel-like way do form an umbelliform inflorescence. The cymose detail is lost, but the class is true. Limit the rule to inflorescences.
'Coniferous' describes a taxon or a type of forest, not a part that has a strobilus. Strobilus present (PO_0025083) does not fit any bearer.

In floras the phrase is used as 'X continuous in color with Y', meaning the two parts share the same colour. That is concolorous (FLOPO_0991069: the parts compared have the same colour). The 'unbroken stripe' reading is rare.
Prolate means a long, stretched-out ellipsoid, the opposite of broad. Elliptic has ellipsoid as a synonym and is true of a broad ellipsoid.
Exfoliating (FLOPO_0991021) is defined for bark and axes that carry it. On leaves or other surfaces, 'scaling' can mean covered with scales.
Brown-dotted parts are punctate (PATO_0001512), so the class is true. The dot colour is extra detail that a colour pattern can add. Losing it does not make the rule wrong.
Not fragrant does not mean odourless (PATO_0001208). The part may smell bad or have some other smell. There is no fragrant class to negate (fragrant is only a related synonym of sweet-scented).
Tripinnate (FLOPO_0991159) is wrong twice: it means divided into leaflets, not cut into lobes, and three times rather than four. Four times pinnatifid is still pinnatifid. No four-times class exists.
Pseudo-fascicled means the parts only look clustered and are not truly fascicled (FLOPO_0991098). No 'pseudofasciculate' class exists, unlike pseudoverticillate.
'Venulose' describes conspicuous, dense fine veinlets. Every leaf has vascular bundles (PO_0005020) and veinlets, so a presence statement adds nothing and misses the point.
Broadest at the middle covers elliptic, oblong, orbicular and linear shapes. It says where the widest point is, not which shape the part has.

Mucronate (FLOPO_0991054) is defined as ending abruptly in a short, narrow, stiff point. A pungent apiculus is exactly that, so stiffness is kept and only the sharpness is underplayed. The class is true.

'Not sharp' (PATO_0001419) is right when 'pungent' means sharp-pointed. It is wrong when 'pungent' describes a smell or taste (compare spicy-scented, FLOPO_0991017). Limit the rule to parts with points.
Doubly serrate means teeth that carry smaller teeth, with no size limit. Its synonyms include the biserrulate forms, so doubly serrulate belongs there and the double toothing is kept.
Incised-serrate means deeply, sharply serrate, so serrated (PATO_0001206) is true. PATO cut (PATO_0001978) means divided by deep regular cuts, which is a different statement. Only the depth is lost.
Sarcotestal means the seed has a fleshy seed coat. Fleshy (PATO_0002351) is true of the testa (PO_0020057) or seed coat (PO_0009088), and loosely of the seed.
The prominence belongs to the veins, not to the part described. It needs a vein + prominent pattern (vascular bundle PO_0005020 with prominent PATO_0001482), not a word rule on the part.
The word is ambiguous: 'glandular and hairless' or 'without glandular hairs'. Rejecting it is better than a guess.
Corolla spur absent (PO_0025512) is right only when the spur in question belongs to the corolla or petals. On the calyx, sepals or other parts it would point to the wrong spur.
Short-caulescent is used in contrast to acaulescent. Its main point is that a stem exists, so stem present (PO_0009047) is true. The shortness is detail that is lost.
'Irregularly cut' also covers incised, laciniate and erose margins, not just torn-looking ones (lacerate, FLOPO_0991115). PATO cut (PATO_0001978) requires regular cuts, so it does not fit either.
Bicucullate means the part carries two hoods. The part itself is not hood-shaped, so cucullate (FLOPO_0991119) on it is wrong, and no existing class means 'two-hooded'.
